newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela blows-up its most infamous prison.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela blows-up its most infamous prison.

text.p: Venezuela's President Rafael Caldera blew-up on Sunday the country's most infamous prison Catia, reducing to rubble in less than two seconds its 31 year record of horror and squalor.

Thousands of on-lookers cheered as clouds of grayish dust ballooned into the clear blue sky, obliterating the remains of the white bricked-building that had come to symbolise everything wrong with Venezuela's crammed and violent jails.

"This is an important symbolic moment ... we'll convert this space into one of culture, dialogue, peace," said Justice Minister Enrique Meier before Caldera flicked the red switch on a small radio detonator linked to 110 kilograms (220 lbs) of dynamite.
Commonly referred to as "Hell", or the "Monster", the Reten de Catia was built 31 years ago in western Caracas for 750 inmates but in recent months held up to 2,000. It was violent to the end.

In 1996, Pope John Paul II blessed what he thought were inmates waving handkerchiefs and Vatican and Venezuelan flags from their cells. The prison's chaplain later said the "inmates" were in fact police officers, causing a major embarrassment to the government.

"Catia was only 10 minutes from central Caracas, but it might as well have been on Mars," said leading Venezuelan artist Jacobo Borges whose museum abutts onto the site. The Venezuelan pavilion exhibited in Seville in 1992 to celebrate Columbus' discovery of the Americas will be erected in its place.

Meir acknowledged in his short speech there was still much to do to improve Venezuela's jails, considered the worst in Latin America, and he promised more would be built to ease chronic overcrowding. Catia's 1,800 prisoners were transferred to two new penitentiaries in January.
In a report published on Friday, U.S. based group Human Rights Watch said over three people are killed and 20 wounded each week in Venezuela's jails.
With only one guard per 150 prisoners, mafias rule, inmates openly walk around with home-made guns, knives and machetes, and young prisoners are turned into sex slaves.
One prisoner at La Planta jail in central Caracas, where 25 died last year in a fire started by prison guards, told the report's interviewers prisoners killed for as little as 50 bolivars (10 cents).

Originally built for 15,000 prisoners, Venezuela's 32 jails now hold over 24,000. Of those, only one in four have been sentenced, the report said. The rest wait up to five years for trial at the hands of a judicial system widely considered grossly inefficient and corrupt.
